1198.title: Ja'far al-Sadiq's school
1198.hook: the Ja'fari school, followed by Twelver Shia, is named for the sixth Imam
1198.carry: the school of the sixth imam
1198.howItsDone: Twelver Shia Muslims follow the Ja'fari school of law, which draws on the Qur'an, the sunnah of the Prophet and the teachings of the Imams, and Sunni scholars also honor Ja'far al-Sadiq as a scholar of the Prophet's household.

segments.voice: Yesterday: where it's followed, the Hanbali lands of Saudi Arabia and Qatar. Your line: the smallest, the steadfast.

Sahih Muslim holds a long report of the Prophet's pilgrimage, told step by step, from setting out to the standing at Arafat. Look at who passed it on: Ja'far ibn Muhammad, from his father, from the Companion Jabir ibn 'Abd Allah. Sunni hadith scholars carried that report through him, and call him al-Sadiq, the truthful. For Twelver Shia Muslims he is also Imam Ja'far al-Sadiq, the sixth Imam. One man, honored on both sides. Today, the school of law that carries his name.

segments.voice: You met him on day 894, beside his father. The Ja'fari school is the school of law followed by Twelver Shia Muslims. Twelvers recognize a line of Imams from the Prophet's family, beginning with 'Ali, and Ja'far is the sixth. He lived and taught in Medina, after his father, Muhammad al-Baqir. Shia tradition holds that the Imams carry the Prophet's knowledge, passed from one to the next, and that Ja'far taught openly, on law, on the Qur'an, on belief, which is why the school bears his name. Sunni Muslims honor him too, as a scholar of the Prophet's household. Reports say Abu Hanifa and Malik sat with him or learned from him; scholars weigh those reports differently. From inside, its sources are the Qur'an and the sunnah. For Twelvers, the sunnah includes the teachings of the Imams, received through Shia collections such as al-Kafi, gathered by al-Kulayni. It uses reason, 'aql, which this block met a few weeks ago. And its jurists don't use analogy, qiyas, the way the Sunni schools do; in Shia reports, Ja'far himself warns against it. One saying attributed to him in al-Kafi, paraphrased: don't judge a man by how long he bows and prostrates; that may be a habit he'd feel lost without. Look instead at his truthfulness when he speaks, and at how he returns what was entrusted to him. Two plain things: the word you give, and the thing you were trusted with.

segments.voice: Say his saying in your own words: don't judge by the length of the bowing; look at truthful speech and a trust returned. Don't fix it yet; just see it and breathe, and if you pray, you can ask to be trustworthy.

1199.title: The source of emulation
1199.hook: Twelver Shia follow a living senior jurist, a marja', in matters of law
1199.howItsDone: Twelver Shia Muslims choose a living marja' whose practical rulings they follow, consulting his book of rulings, his website or his offices with questions about prayer, fasting, trade and daily life.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the Ja'fari school, named for Ja'far al-Sadiq. Your line: the school of the sixth imam.

On a shelf in a Shia home there may be a thick paperback of numbered rulings. Prayer. Fasting. Buying and selling. Travel. What to do if you lose count in the middle of a prayer. The author's name is on the cover, and he's alive. Next door, the shelf may hold the same kind of book by a different author. Each adult in the family may have chosen their own. Today, the living person a believer follows, and why that person has to be living.
screen: `A PAPERBACK OF NUMBERED RULINGS.` → `A LIVING NAME ON THE COVER.` → `CHOSEN BY EACH ADULT.`

segments.voice: The word is marja': a reference, a place you turn to. In full, marja' al-taqlid, the source of emulation; taqlid means following someone else's ruling. Ja'fari books of practical rulings open with a choice. In matters of law, an adult can take one of three roads. Become a mujtahid, a jurist able to derive rulings from the sources. Act with precaution, doing what satisfies every serious opinion, which takes a good deal of knowledge too. Or follow a mujtahid, the road these books expect someone without that training to take. The one followed is the marja'. The books list what he must be: adult, sane, just, a Twelver Shia, and a mujtahid. And they add: as best you can tell, follow the most learned, by asking people of knowledge you trust. Then the condition in today's line: living. In these books, you may not begin following a scholar who has already died. The reason Shia jurists give: the law keeps meeting new questions, new medicines, new machines, new kinds of money, and a living jurist can answer them. The door of reasoning stays open. Whether you may stay with a marja' who died while you followed him, they answer differently, and that's a question for your living marja'. This following has limits. It covers practical law: how to pray, fast, trade. The books ask each person to reach the foundations of belief for themselves. Shia jurists explain taqlid with a familiar picture: the one who doesn't know turns to the one who does, the way a patient turns to a doctor.
screen: `MARJA': A SOURCE TO TURN TO.` · `THREE ROADS: REASON, CAUTION, FOLLOW.` · `LEARNED, JUST, AND LIVING.` · `A PATIENT AND A DOCTOR.`

segments.voice: Say the three roads slowly: derive it, be cautious, or follow someone who can. Then think of one person you lean on who knows more than you, a doctor, a mechanic, an aunt who knows the family recipes, and ask how you chose them and what would make you stop trusting them. Hold them in mind for a few breaths with some gratitude, and if you pray, you can ask for good guides.
Marja'. A source to turn to: in Twelver Shia law, the living senior jurist whose practical rulings a believer follows. Today's word.
Your line: follow the living scholar. New questions keep coming, and a living jurist can answer them. Go gently.

1200.title: The seminaries
1200.hook: the great seminaries of Najaf and Qom
1200.howItsDone: Shia students study at the seminaries of Najaf, Qom and elsewhere, moving from Arabic and logic through set textbooks to advanced lectures beyond the textbook, often reviewing in pairs.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the marja', the living scholar a believer follows. Your line: follow the living scholar.

Morning, in a narrow lane near a golden dome. Two students sit on a mat with one book open between them. One reads a line and explains it. The other objects. The first pushes back, finds the line again, reads it more slowly. Nobody is angry. This is the work. Yesterday's marja' doesn't appear out of nowhere. He is made, over long years, in lanes and rooms like this one. Today, the places that make them.
screen: `TWO STUDENTS, ONE BOOK.` → `READ, OBJECT, PUSH BACK.` → `WHERE A MARJA' IS MADE.`

segments.voice: The word is hawzah, the Shia seminary; in full, al-hawzah al-'ilmiyyah, the seat of learning. Today's two cities are Najaf and Qom. Najaf, in Iraq, is the city of the shrine of Imam 'Ali. Tradition says its hawzah grew around the scholar Shaykh al-Tusi, who settled there after leaving Baghdad. Qom, in Iran, holds the shrine of Fatimah al-Ma'sumah, sister of Imam al-Rida, and its hawzah was revived in modern times. Both are shrine cities; the study happens in the shadow of the domes. It runs in stages, not fixed years. First the preliminaries: Arabic grammar, logic, rhetoric. Then the surfaces, the sutuh: set textbooks of law and its method, read line by line with a teacher. Then the highest stage, bahth al-kharij, study outside the text: a senior teacher lectures on a question with no set book, weighing the evidence and earlier opinions aloud, and students are expected to argue back. Between lessons, students review in pairs, like the two on the mat. A student chooses teachers, sits in their circles, moves on when ready. Out of long years of that comes a mujtahid. And from among the mujtahids, through the regard of other scholars and the trust of believers, a marja'. Scholars move between the two cities; a student may begin in one and finish in the other. In this telling, Najaf and Qom aren't rivals. They're two lamps in the same tradition, on either side of a border.
screen: `HAWZAH: THE SEAT OF LEARNING.` · `NAJAF AND QOM, TWO SHRINE CITIES.` · `GRAMMAR, TEXTBOOKS, BEYOND THE TEXT.` · `FROM STUDENT TO MUJTAHID TO MARJA'.`

segments.voice: On a map or in your mind, find Baghdad and follow south to Najaf, and notice the town beside it: Kufa, Abu Hanifa's city, two schools as close neighbors. Then cross east into Iran and find Qom, south of Tehran, resting a few breaths on each city. Last, think of one place where you were really taught something, a classroom, a kitchen, a garage, and if you pray, you can remember your teachers.

1201.title: Praying on earth
1201.hook: Shia in the Ja'fari school prostrate on earth, often on a small clay tablet from Karbala
1201.howItsDone: Shia Muslims who follow the Ja'fari school prostrate on earth or on what grows from it, often placing a small clay tablet, a turbah, sometimes made from the soil of Karbala, where the forehead rests.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the hawzah, the seminaries of Najaf and Qom. Your line: najaf and qom.

A night of rain in Medina. The mosque's roof is palm branches, and it leaks. At the dawn prayer the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, goes down in prostration onto ground that has turned to mud. The Companion Abu Sa'id al-Khudri says that afterward he saw the trace of mud and water on the Prophet's forehead. The report sits in Sahih al-Bukhari. Keep that forehead in mind. Today is about what it touches.
screen: `RAIN THROUGH A PALM-BRANCH ROOF.` → `MUD ON THE PROPHET'S FOREHEAD.` → `WHAT THE FOREHEAD TOUCHES.`

segments.voice: Day 901 met the turbah in passing; here's the fuller story. The word means soil, earth, and here, a small object. In the Ja'fari school, the forehead in prostration has to rest on the earth itself, or on something that grows from the earth, as long as it isn't eaten or worn. Bare ground, stone, sand, a mat woven of palm leaves: yes. A wool carpet, a cotton cloth: not for the forehead. So in a carpeted mosque or a living room, you bring a little earth with you: a small tablet of baked clay, round or square, set where the forehead will land. Some are plain clay. Some are pressed from the soil of Karbala, where the Prophet's grandson, Imam Husayn, was killed, and they carry that memory into every prayer. A turbah is not something prayed to. It's something prayed on. The prostration is to God; the clay is only what the forehead touches. Shia jurists point to the Prophet's own practice, the mud on his forehead, and to the report, also in Sahih al-Bukhari, that the earth has been made for him a place of prayer and a means of purification. They cite reports from the Imams as well. Sunni schools read the evidence differently. They allow prostration on a carpet or cloth, citing, among other reports, Companions who spread part of their garment and prostrated on it in fierce heat. Shia jurists read that as an allowance for need. Both sides share the same scene: the highest part of the body lowered to the ground. They differ on what may lie between.
screen: `TURBAH: SOIL, EARTH.` · `EARTH, OR WHAT GROWS FROM IT.` · `PRAYED ON, NOT PRAYED TO.` · `SAME SCENE, A DIFFERENT READING.`

segments.voice: If you can, find some clean earth, a plant pot, a stone on the windowsill, even a plain clay mug, and rest your fingertips on it, noticing its temperature, its grain, whether it's damp or dry. If there's none nearby, rest your palm flat on the floor and picture the soil somewhere underneath, the lowest thing in the room, met on purpose. If you pray, you can remember the One the forehead bows to.

1202.title: Three times of prayer
1202.hook: Shia usually combine the five prayers into three times of day, which Sunni schools allow in certain cases
1202.howItsDone: Twelver Shia follow Ja'fari law, which lets noon and afternoon, and sunset and night, be prayed together, so the five prayers are often prayed in three sittings; Sunni schools join prayers for set reasons such as travel, rain, or the pilgrimage.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the turbah, a small tablet of clay, and your line: forehead on earth.

A family in Detroit finishes lunch, and someone lays out the prayer mats. They pray the noon prayer, then the afternoon prayer straight after it. That evening, the same: sunset, then night, back to back. Their neighbor down the street, who also prays five times a day, waits for the afternoon prayer until the shadows grow long. Same Qur'an, same five prayers, same direction. Two different clocks. Neither family is cutting corners. Each follows a school, and each school can show you its reasons.
screen: `NOON, THEN AFTERNOON, BACK TO BACK.` → `A NEIGHBOR WAITS FOR THE SHADOWS.` → `FIVE PRAYERS, TWO CLOCKS.`

segments.voice: Start with the common ground. The Qur'an says, in Pickthall's words, "Lo! worship at fixed hours hath been enjoined on the believers." The prayers have times. The question is how wide those times are. Next, a verse the schools read differently. In surah seventeen, the Qur'an tells the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ to establish prayer from the sun's decline until the dark of night, and the recitation at dawn. Some readers hear three moments there: the decline of the sun, the dark of night, and dawn. Then a report. In Sahih Muslim, Ibn Abbas says the Prophet prayed noon and afternoon together, and sunset and night together, in Medina, with no fear and no rain. Asked why, Ibn Abbas said he wanted no hardship for his community. Ja'fari scholars, followed by Twelver Shia, read the verse and the report together: noon and afternoon share one stretch of time, and so do sunset and night. Praying each at its own moment is good, they teach, and joining is permitted any day. So a Shia family can pray the five in three sittings: dawn, midday, evening. The Sunni schools know the same report, and they also allow joining, called jam', but for set reasons. Shafi'i, Maliki and Hanbali scholars allow it on a journey, and some for heavy rain or illness. Hanafi scholars allow it on pilgrimage, at Arafah and Muzdalifah. Otherwise, each prayer keeps its own time. Two readings of the same texts: one widens the time, the other keeps each prayer in its own.
screen: `COMMON GROUND: PRAYER HAS FIXED HOURS.` · `ONE VERSE, READ AS THREE MOMENTS.` · `IBN ABBAS: JOINED, IN MEDINA, NO RAIN.` · `SUNNI SCHOOLS: JOIN FOR SET REASONS.`

segments.voice: Think back over yesterday and count, on your fingers, the moments your day paused: at dawn, at lunch, at a red light, or only at night. If you pray, notice which prayers you pray in their own moment and which you gather together, and where your school draws that line; if you don't, notice where your day already stops, the places a prayer could sit. No judging, just counting.

1203.howItsDone: Zaydi Muslims, found mainly in the northern highlands of Yemen, follow a Shia school named for Zayd ibn Ali; they hold that an imam must be a learned descendant of Ali and Fatima who comes forward openly, and their law is close to the Sunni schools in much.

segments.voice: Yesterday, three times of prayer: all five prayers, in three sittings. Your line: five in three.

What does the word Shia mean? Party, or followers. Tradition gives the full phrase as shi'at Ali, the party of Ali, the Prophet's cousin and son-in-law. But the party has more than one house. Yesterday's three sittings belong to the Twelvers. Today's house grew up in the highlands of Yemen, with law a visitor from a Sunni mosque would recognize. Its people are named for one man, a great-grandson of Ali, who stood up in Kufa when he believed the rulers of his day had gone wrong. His name was Zayd.
screen: `SHIA: THE PARTY OF ALI.` → `MORE THAN ONE HOUSE.` → `A MAN NAMED ZAYD.`

segments.voice: Zayd ibn Ali was a grandson of Husayn, the grandson of the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ. Tradition says he was known for learning and prayer, and that he rose against the Umayyad rulers in Kufa and was killed there. Those who held to his example became the Zaydis. Next, what makes a leader. For Twelvers, the imams are named one by one, each designated by the one before, and the twelfth is in hiding. Zaydi teaching draws the line differently. An imam must be a descendant of Ali and Fatima, learned enough to judge, upright, and willing to come forward openly and call people to what is right. The Qur'an speaks of a community that will "enjoin right conduct and forbid indecency." Zaydi scholars hear a duty there: a qualified leader doesn't wait in silence. Then the law. In much of the law of prayer, fasting and trade, Zaydi rulings sit near the Sunni schools, and Zaydi scholars have long read and argued with Hanafi and Shafi'i books. Tradition says Zayd himself refused to condemn the first caliphs, Abu Bakr and Umar: Ali was the better choice, he held, and the others still led. That stance has made the Zaydis a kind of bridge, close to both neighbors and identical to neither. Last, the place. For a long stretch of history, Zaydi imams led communities in the mountains of northern Yemen, around towns like Sa'dah and Sana'a. The school is still there, in the mosques and schools of those highlands.
screen: `ZAYD IBN ALI ROSE IN KUFA.` · `AN IMAM WHO COMES FORWARD OPENLY.` · `LAW CLOSE TO SUNNI NEIGHBORS.` · `THE HIGHLANDS OF YEMEN.`

segments.voice: Find Yemen in your mind, at the bottom corner of the Arabian peninsula, the Red Sea to the west and the Gulf of Aden to the south, then go up, off the coast, into the mountains: terraced fields, stone towers, towns built high. That's where the Zaydi school grew. If you pray, you can remember the people of Yemen in your prayer; if not, just rest on that mountain picture and breathe.
The Zaydis. A Shia school named for Zayd ibn Ali, rooted in the highlands of Yemen, with law close to the Sunni schools in much. Today's word.
Your line: the zaydis. The word Shia names more than one house, and this is one. Until tomorrow.

1204.title: The Ibadis
1204.hook: the school of Oman and parts of North Africa, which rejects the Kharijite label
1204.howItsDone: Ibadi Muslims, centered in Oman with communities in North Africa and East Africa, follow their own school of law and theology; they reject being called Kharijites and hold that other Muslims remain within the faith.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Zaydis of Yemen, proof that Shia names more than one house. Your line: the zaydis.

A nickname nobody asked for. It sticks at school, at work, in the family. It comes from an old story, or from somebody else's mistake, and the person wearing it wants to say: that's not me. Now stretch that across a whole community and a long history. A school of Islam, rooted in Oman and in pockets of North Africa, has been handed a label in other people's books. Its scholars have spent a long time answering, patiently: that's not us. Today, the Ibadis, and the name they refuse.
screen: `A NICKNAME NOBODY ASKED FOR.` → `A WHOLE SCHOOL, ONE LABEL.` → `THAT'S NOT US.`

segments.voice: Tradition says the school is named for Abd Allah ibn Ibad, an early figure in Basra, and Ibadis also honor a scholar of that city, Jabir ibn Zayd, as a teacher at their root. Now the label. In the early civil wars, a group broke away from Ali's camp. Others called them the Khawarij, those who went out. Some of them declared other Muslims unbelievers and treated their blood as lawful. Some writers outside the school filed the Ibadis under that same heading. Ibadi scholars answer that the extremists who killed other Muslims were wrong, and that their own teachers broke from them over exactly that. To an Ibadi, other Muslims stay inside the faith: people to live beside, pray near and trade with. And there's a verse they can point to. The Qur'an says, in Pickthall's words, "neither defame one another, nor insult one another by nicknames." A label used to push someone out of the community is the kind of thing that line warns against. Last, the place. In Oman the Ibadi school has deep roots, with its own scholars, mosques and law. It's also found in parts of North Africa, in desert valleys and on islands, and in communities along the East African coast. Its jurists write their own books of fiqh, with their own methods, and they can tell you exactly where they differ from their neighbors and where they agree. A school with its own name, asking to be called by it.
screen: `NAMED FOR ABD ALLAH IBN IBAD.` · `THE LABEL: THOSE WHO WENT OUT.` · `NOT BY NICKNAMES.` · `OMAN AND NORTH AFRICA.`

segments.voice: Say the pair once, slowly: Ibadi, Oman, and let it settle as a name, not a label. Then think of one person you've known only by a label, a coworker, a neighbor, a group in the news, and quietly say the name they'd choose for themselves. If you pray, you can remember them in your prayer.
The Ibadis. The school of Oman and parts of North Africa, which counts other Muslims inside the faith and rejects the Kharijite label. Today's word.
Your line: the ibadis of oman. That closes a week of other houses, from the Ja'fari school to the Ibadis. Rest well.
